articles.title: Scientists found that coffee changes gut microbes linked to mood and brain function; both caffeinated and decaf coffee were associated with lower stress, depression and impulsivity in a new study
articles.summary: Not just the caffeine. A new study reported by ScienceDaily suggests coffee may affect the brain through the gut.
articles.body: Not just the caffeine. A new study reported by ScienceDaily suggests coffee may affect the brain through the gut. Researchers at APC Microbiome Ireland and University College Cork discovered that both caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee were associated with alterations in gut microbes and metabolites linked to mood, stress and cognitive function. Those who resumed coffee drinking after a two-week break reported lower levels of perceived stress, depression and impulsivity. The findings, published in Nature Communications, also showed differences between regular and decaffeinated coffee, with decaf associated with better learning and memory, and caffeinated coffee with less anxiety and better attention. However, the study was small and does not prove that coffee directly improves mental health.Looking beyond caffeineCoffee is often viewed as a quick way to feel more awake, particularly at the start of a demanding day. Its effects, however, may extend well beyond alertness. Coffee contains caffeine, but it also includes polyphenols, phenolic acids and other plant compounds that can interact with the body’s metabolism and the microorganisms living in the digestive system.The study explored the microbiota-gut-brain axis, the two-way communication network connecting the gut and the brain. Signals can travel between these systems through the immune system, hormones, nerves and chemicals produced when gut microbes process food and drinks. That suggests changes in the gut microbiome could affect mood, stress responses and parts of cognition, although scientists are still working out how exactly it does so.To study this connection, researchers studied 31 habitual coffee drinkers and 31 people who didn’t regularly drink coffee. Three to five cups a day was the usual intake for regular coffee drinkers. They first stopped drinking coffee for two weeks, allowing researchers to observe what changed when coffee was removed from their routines. Coffee was then added back for 21 days, with participants receiving either caffeinated or decaffeinated coffee without knowing which type they were drinking, as per the report.Mood changes after coffee returnedWhen coffee was reintroduced, both groups reported lower scores for perceived stress, depression and impulsivity. This was one of the most significant findings because it suggests that some of coffee’s possible effects on mood may not depend entirely on caffeine. If caffeine were responsible for every change, researchers would not necessarily expect decaffeinated coffee to show similar associations.The findings also suggested that regular and decaffeinated coffee may have different effects on people. Those who drank caffeinated coffee reported feeling less anxious and less psychologically distressed. Caffeinated coffee has also been linked to greater vigilance and attention. Decaffeinated coffee, meanwhile, was linked to improvements in learning and episodic memory, as well as better sleep quality and increased physical activity.These findings should be taken with caution. The study involved a small number of people and the participants were healthy adults. Also, some memory improvements could have been affected by better sleep, more physical activity or familiarity with the tests. The researchers also relied partly on questionnaires, which measure how participants felt and behaved but cannot capture every aspect of mental health.Gut bacteria react to coffeeThe researchers found that coffee drinking was associated with changes in some gut bacteria, including Eggertella species and Cryptobacterium curtum. They also noticed changes in members of the Firmicutes group.” These changes were not just a general increase in microbial diversity. Instead, coffee appeared to influence particular strains within the gut community.The study also identified changes in metabolites, which are small molecules made or changed in the course of metabolism. Some of the compounds seemed to be coming directly from coffee itself, while others were linked to the activity of gut microbes. Caffeine-related chemicals appeared in the caffeinated coffee group, but several coffee-related phenolic compounds changed after both caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee were consumed.This may help explain why decaf appeared to have effects of its own. Coffee’s non-caffeine compounds can be processed by gut bacteria, and the resulting metabolites may influence biological pathways involved in inflammation, mood and brain function. The researchers found statistical links between certain microbial species, metabolites and cognitive or behavioural measures, but these links do not yet establish a direct cause.What the study does not proveThe findings do not mean that coffee can prevent depression, treat anxiety or replace professional mental health care. They also do not suggest that everyone should begin drinking several cups of coffee each day. A person’s response to coffee can depend on genetics, sleep, diet, medication, caffeine sensitivity and existing medical conditions.Too much caffeine may cause restlessness, digestive discomfort, a racing heartbeat or difficulty sleeping. For some people, especially those who are sensitive to caffeine, these effects may outweigh any possible benefits. Decaffeinated coffee may be a suitable alternative for people who enjoy the flavour and routine of coffee but want to reduce caffeine intake, although it is not automatically appropriate for every individual.The study was sponsored by the Institute for Scientific Information on Coffee, and its authors acknowledge that the sample size was limited. Larger and longer studies will be needed to determine whether the changes observed in the gut actually lead to improvements in mood or cognition, or whether coffee drinking is simply associated with other healthy habits.A more complex picture of coffeeThe research adds to evidence that coffee is more than a source of caffeine. Its compounds may interact with gut microbes, metabolism, the immune system and the nervous system in ways that differ between individuals. The results also show why researchers are increasingly examining ordinary foods and drinks through the lens of the gut-brain connection.For people who already like coffee, the study offers an interesting explanation as to why the beverage may affect energy, stress and concentration in different ways. The safest takeaway is not to treat coffee as a cure-all, but as one part of a balanced lifestyle that includes adequate sleep, nutritious food, movement and appropriate mental health support.

articles.title: Archaeologists have uncovered a 4,000-year-old Egyptian tomb belonging to an official described as the “keeper of the king's secrets”; the burial contains clues to one of the kingdom's most powerful officials
articles.summary: Beneath the ancient landscape of Saqqara, where generations of Egyptians buried their dead, archaeologists have uncovered a tomb that offers a glimpse
articles.body: Beneath the ancient landscape of Saqqara, where generations of Egyptians buried their dead, archaeologists have uncovered a tomb that offers a glimpse into the world of royal power more than 4,000 years ago. The burial belonged to Sakhnetio-Btah, a senior official whose titles placed him close to the centre of the Old Kingdom administration. According to a latest report by Daily Mail, the discovery at the Bubasteion Necropolis includes a funerary chapel, ritual objects, burial shafts and several remarkably preserved artefacts, helping researchers piece together how elite Egyptians prepared for death and how the site was used long after Sakhnetio-Btah was buried.A man trusted by the kingAs per the report, Hieroglyphic inscriptions inside the tomb helped identify its owner and revealed the range of positions he held during his lifetime. Among them was the striking title of “keeper of the king's secrets”. Rather than suggesting that Sakhnetio-Btah guarded mysterious treasures, the title is understood to have referred to his access to confidential royal documents and decrees. His responsibilities extended well beyond that role. He served as a royal chamberlain, a priest associated with the goddess Maat and a supervisor of the royal library, placing him among the senior figures within the administrative structure of the Old Kingdom. The collection of titles provides an unusual window into the hierarchy surrounding the pharaoh and the responsibilities entrusted to officials operating within the royal court.A symbolic doorway to the afterlifeAlso, the Daily Mail report states that the tomb contains the remains of a funerary chapel and a false door, one of the most recognisable features of ancient Egyptian burial architecture. These structures were more than decorative elements. The false door was understood as a symbolic passage between the world of the living and the realm of the dead, allowing the deceased to receive offerings and maintain a connection with the living world. Archaeologists also found an offering table, an offering slab and a purification basin. Their discovery in their original positions is particularly valuable because it preserves evidence of how funerary rituals were organised and carried out.Burials reveal a changing necropolisSurrounding Sakhnetio-Btah's tomb is a network of interconnected burial shafts containing numerous human remains and painted funerary cartonnage. The colourful coverings, made from layers of material resembling papier-mâché, were placed over mummies and commonly decorated with gods, hieroglyphs and scenes associated with the journey into the afterlife. More than 100 ushabti figurines were also recovered. These small figures were intended to perform tasks for the deceased in the afterlife, reflecting the elaborate preparations made for continued existence beyond death, adds the report. Among the most significant discoveries were three stone sarcophagi that remained sealed and intact in their original locations. A wooden falcon statue, pottery vessels and other artefacts added to the collection. Some sections of the complex appear to have been looted in antiquity, but many surviving objects remain in unusually good condition.Saqqara's archaeological treasure troveThe discovery adds another layer to Saqqara, one of Egypt's most important archaeological landscapes. The vast necropolis is home to the Step Pyramid of Djoser, Egypt's oldest pyramid, built roughly 4,700 years ago, as well as thousands of tombs associated with rulers, priests, nobles and officials. Recent excavations at the site have revealed sealed coffins, animal cemeteries, mummification workshops and richly decorated burial shafts. Together, these discoveries have expanded knowledge of not only Egypt's rulers but also the religious customs, occupations and daily lives surrounding death. As excavation continues around the newly uncovered tomb, researchers expect the surrounding burial network to provide further evidence of how Saqqara evolved and was repeatedly reused across different periods of Egyptian history.Images Courtesy: Daily Mail

articles.title: Meet Tiffani Gay, the student whose electromagnet prototype removed nearly 93% of oil from polluted water
articles.summary: The project focuses on separating non-surface crude oil from water, an area the ISEF abstract describes as having limited research.
articles.body: The project focuses on separating non-surface crude oil from water, an area the ISEF abstract describes as having limited research. Tiffani Gay, a student researcher from Orlando Science Schools, developed a prototype that uses an electromagnetic field and a specialised magnetorheological fluid to separate oil from water. Her project, “Year II: Resistant Electromagnet Propulsion for Petroleum Removal Employing Biocompatible Magnetorheological Fluid in Oil Spill Applications,” was presented in the Environmental Engineering category at the 2024 Regeneron International Science and Engineering Fair. According to the official ISEF project abstract, the project reported approximately 92.8% oil removal under its most effective reported condition, which used a 1:4 concentration of the magnetorheological fluid in distilled water. The project received the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Taking the Pulse of the Planet First Award.Tiffani Gay and electromagnetic oil separation: how the prototype worksGay's research focuses on the separation of non-surface crude oil from water. The ISEF abstract says the prototype connects an oil-and-water solution to an electromagnetic-field separation tube. When the electromagnetic coils were discharged, the system produced a propulsive effect that separated the oil and water. The process uses a specialised magnetorheological fluid, or MRF, containing iron oxide, specifically Fe3O4 microspheres, suspended in oleic acid. The project describes the fluid as viscoelastic and reports that it exhibited super lipophilicity and hydrophobicity,’ as described in the project abstract. When added to the petroleum-and-water solution, the MRF gave the mixture magnetic properties that allowed the electromagnetic field to act on it during the separation process.Electromagnetic separation removed 88.5% of oil after 14 minutesThe project's reported results varied depending on the test conditions. The ISEF abstract reports that the EMF system was most effective at 14 minutes, when it removed 88.5% of the oil. The abstract also reports that there was no significant relationship between the type of water used in the experiment, with both seawater and distilled water tested. The highest reported removal rate came when the magnetorheological fluid was used at a 1:4 concentration in a distilled-water environment. Under those conditions, approximately 92.8% of the oil was removed. This is the headline result from the project, but it represents the outcome of the reported experimental conditions rather than evidence that the prototype can remove the same proportion of oil from an actual marine spill. The distinction matters because the project was a prototype study. The ISEF abstract reports successful oil separation in the experimental system, while the proposed applications would require the technology to be developed and tested beyond the conditions used in the project.Where Tiffani Gay's oil-separation system could be usedThe project abstract identifies several possible applications for the technology. It says the approach could potentially be used for pollution-control applications involving polyatomic hydrocarbons, microplastics and organic pharmaceutical compounds. These are presented as potential applications of the research rather than demonstrated results from the prototype. Gay's proposed deployment options include connecting the system to a tube along a shoreline or using a buoy collection mechanism for applications in deeper water. The project also says a deep-learning model based on fluorescence imaging is being investigated to quantify pollution levels and potentially guide targeted use of the system. The official ISEF abstract concludes that the device met its engineering goals by introducing a method of oil-spill removal based on electromagnetics. The reported results provide a proof of concept for the prototype under the tested conditions, while further development would be needed to determine how the system performs in larger or more complex environments.

articles.title: Arqueologia e Indiana Jones: os mitos e a realidade da ciência | G1
articles.standfirst: A cultura pop desperta interesse pelo passado, mas reforça a ideia de caça ao tesouro e apaga anos de pesquisa, análise e debate científico.
articles.summary: A arqueologia real substitui o chicote de Indiana Jones por anos de pesquisa científica e análises rigorosas para desvendar a história humana.
articles.body:
Harrison Ford em “Os Caçadores da Arca Perdida”: embora personagem seja o mais conhecido atualmente, associação da arqueologia com uma vida de aventuras remonta às explorações coloniais do século XIX, quando o passado era tratado menos como conhecimento e mais como saque — Foto: Landmark Media

Quando arqueólogos egípcios anunciaram a descoberta de uma “cidade dourada perdida” perto de Luxor, no Egito, em 2021, as manchetes explodiram em todo o mundo: Tesouro. Revelação. Um achado que só acontece uma vez a cada século.

Para os arqueólogos, no entanto, o aspecto mais notável não foi o ouro que ainda não havia dado as caras, mas a rapidez com que a história foi transformada em uma aventura. Anos de levantamentos, mapeamento estratigráfico e análise de cerâmicas quase não foram mencionados.

A arqueologia é uma das raras disciplinas em que a cultura popular não reflete simplesmente a compreensão do público, mas a produz ativamente. Muitas pessoas entram em contato com a arqueologia não por meio de relatórios de escavações ou catálogos de museus, mas por meio de um homem de chapéu fedora estalando um chicote em uma tumba iluminada por tochas.

Em minhas discussões sobre arqueologia e cultura popular na Universidade de Tübingen, isso fica imediatamente claro. Os alunos raramente chegam com expectativas moldadas por relatórios de sítios arqueológicos ou literatura especializada — eles chegam com “Indiana Jones”.

A ideia da arqueologia como aventura é anterior à própria disciplina. Ela surgiu a partir das explorações coloniais do século XIX, quando o passado era tratado menos como conhecimento e mais como saque. Sítios antigos eram vistos como reservatórios de objetos exóticos a serem extraídos e exibidos. Ainda antes disso, no século XVII, viajantes como Cornelis de Bruyn voltavam do Levante - região geográfica que engloba o que hoje são a província de Hatay, na Turquia, Síria, Líbano, Israel, Palestina e Jordânia, além de alguma vezes a Cilícia, Chipre e a Península do Sinai - como pequenas celebridades.

A literatura de aventura vitoriana — com destaque para As Minas do Rei Salomão (1885), de H. Rider Haggard — apresentava paisagens distantes como cenários para riquezas ocultas e civilizações perdidas. Mesmo quando a arqueologia se tornou uma disciplina acadêmica, ela permaneceu entrelaçada a essa narrativa. Os museus exibiam artefatos como fragmentos espetaculares de mundos desaparecidos, frequentemente separados de seu contexto arqueológico.

A literatura popular ampliou essa lógica. O livro Deuses, Túmulos e Estudiosos (1949), de C.W. Ceram, transformou a pesquisa arqueológica em uma sequência de descobertas dramáticas. Ele convidou os leitores a vivenciar a escavação como uma série de momentos de revelação. Ao fazer isso, ajudou a consolidar uma forma narrativa específica: a arqueologia como um encontro heroico com o passado, impulsionado por indivíduos excepcionais e achados espetaculares.

O cinema amplificou e padronizou isso. De A Múmia (1932) a Os Caçadores da Arca Perdida (1981) e, posteriormente, Tomb Raider (1996) e Assassin’s Creed (2007), a arqueologia tornou-se um gênero reconhecível, definido por câmaras secretas, armadilhas e heroísmo solitário.

A persistência da narrativa de aventura não é difícil de explicar. A arqueologia lida com material inerentemente cativante: objetos, ruínas, restos mortais. A mídia popular seleciona seus momentos mais cinematográficos — o túmulo desenterrado, a inscrição decifrada, o artefato reluzente — e os apresenta como se fossem a própria história.

Nos filmes de Indiana Jones, o conhecimento surge por meio de revelações. Uma câmara secreta se abre. Um mistério é desvendado. O passado parece ter estado esperando para ser descoberto. Mas a arqueologia real funciona quase ao contrário.

Anos dedicados a documentar paredes em ruínas, fragmentos frágeis de cerâmica e traços tênues de assentamentos raramente produzem momentos espetaculares. O trabalho de campo geralmente ocorre em condições difíceis, sob calor, poeira ou lama, e se desenvolve por meio de medições, registros e interpretações. O conhecimento é construído, não descoberto, e depois discutido, revisado e, às vezes, abandonado. A narrativa de aventura apaga esse processo.

A chamada “cidade dourada perdida” de Áton ilustra essa tensão. Anunciada como uma das descobertas mais significativas no Egito em décadas, ela gerou manchetes em todo o mundo antes mesmo que uma análise substancial tivesse sido publicada. O próprio rótulo “dourada” permaneceu sem explicação. A revelação circulou amplamente; a produção de conhecimento que se seguiu permaneceu lenta e em andamento.

O modelo de aventura também traz implicações éticas. Questões de propriedade, restituição e patrimônio indígena se encaixam de forma incômoda em uma estrutura que trata artefatos como objetos a serem encontrados, em vez de evidências inseridas em contextos culturais e políticos vivos. A figura do escavador ocidental solitário recuperando passados perdidos tem uma genealogia colonial que a arqueologia contemporânea continua a enfrentar.

As plataformas digitais intensificam ainda mais essas dinâmicas. O Instagram e o TikTok privilegiam o imediatismo visual e valorizam os momentos de descoberta em detrimento do trabalho interpretativo de longo prazo. A visibilidade algorítmica tende a favorecer o espetáculo, não o processo.

Mas o mito da aventura não é simplesmente um erro a ser corrigido. Descartá-lo totalmente seria não compreender sua função cultural.

Sem Indiana Jones, muitas pessoas raramente pensariam no passado humano remoto. A frequência a museus, o financiamento para pesquisas e o interesse dos estudantes são, em parte, sustentados por uma imaginação cultural na qual a arqueologia é importante o suficiente para ser empolgante.

No ensino, essa dinâmica é familiar. Os alunos costumam chegar atraídos pela arqueologia cinematográfica, mas muitos partem envolvidos por algo totalmente diferente: a percepção de que o fragmento mais despretensioso de um pote quebrado ou de um objeto desgastado pode reformular a compreensão histórica.

Há também uma dimensão reflexiva nessa história. Os próprios arqueólogos participam da construção das narrativas que circulam sobre seu trabalho. Comunicados à imprensa anunciando “cidades perdidas” ou “descobertas que acontecem uma vez a cada século” não são de autoria de Hollywood. A tensão entre a comunicação pública e a precisão acadêmica é inerente à disciplina.

A maioria das pessoas nunca lerá um relatório de escavação. Sua compreensão da arqueologia é moldada por meio de histórias, não de documentação técnica.

Indiana Jones teria dificuldade em obter uma licença de escavação nos dias de hoje. A maioria das descobertas arqueológicas ocorre longe de templos em ruínas — na análise comparativa, na reavaliação computacional de conjuntos de dados históricos, no lento aperfeiçoamento do consenso acadêmico. Mas a precisão por si só não determina a influência cultural.

O mito da aventura comprime um processo complexo, distribuído e muitas vezes invisível em uma narrativa que pode ser reconhecida à primeira vista. Ele obscurece grande parte do que é a arqueologia, mas também mantém seu lugar no imaginário público.

A questão mais difícil é o que a arqueologia decide fazer com a atenção que gera — e que tipos de histórias ela conta uma vez que a porta tenha sido aberta.

Stephan Blum é pesquisador Associado do Instituto de Pré-História, História Antiga e Arqueologia Medieval da Universidade de Tübingen. Ele não presta consultoria, trabalha, possui ações ou recebe financiamento de qualquer empresa ou organização que poderia se beneficiar com a publicação deste artigo e não revelou nenhum vínculo relevante além de seu cargo acadêmico.

articles.title: DNA evidence from Thomas Jefferson’s hair reveals the truth about his relationship with Sally Hemings
articles.summary: Thomas Jefferson’s DNA sheds new light on his relationship with Sally Hemings and supports the longstanding conclusion that he fathered her children.
articles.body:
Opening a Bible that once belonged to Thomas Jefferson, staff at the Smithsonian National Museum of American History in 2011 discovered a reddish-blond hair pressed between the pages. That hair, suspected to have belonged to Jefferson himself, launched a DNA investigation spanning more than a decade that's now providing a long-missing puzzle piece regarding Jefferson's relationship with Sally Hemings, an enslaved woman in his household.

After spending years reconstructing DNA fragments, scientists have revealed the most compelling evidence to date that Jefferson, a founding father of the United States, also fathered children with Hemings — a relationship that has been long rumored but never definitively proven. How that investigation unfolded is documented in the book " History by a Hair : Thomas Jefferson, Sally Hemings & Solving a 200-Year-Old Mystery," written by Richard Kurin, a distinguished scholar and ambassador-at-large at the Smithsonian, and published on September 22.

Kurin is also senior author of a paper describing the methods that connected the former US president to Hemings' descendants, which involved delving deep into the genetics of the Jefferson and Hemings family trees. The paper, published September 21 on the preprint platform bioRXiv , has not yet been peer-reviewed.

In addition to testing the hair found in the Bible, the researchers also collected genetic material from multiple confirmed samples of Jefferson's hair, held in the collection of the Smithsonian. They compared that with DNA from descendants of multiple lineages: Jefferson and his wife Martha, Jefferson's brother Randolph, and two of Hemings' sons, Eston and Madison. (Hemings had four children who lived to adulthood, but only Eston and Madison claimed Jefferson as their father).

Matches in the DNA suggest the chance that Thomas Jefferson fathered at least one of Sally Hemings' children was 99.96%.

Previously, a genetic study from 1998 led by the late Eugene Foster, a retired pathology professor at Tufts University and the University of Virginia, claimed to prove Jefferson's parentage of Hemings' children. That study found a rare haplotype — a combination of genes — in the Y chromosomes of males descended from Thomas Jefferson's uncle. That same haplotype existed in descendants of Hemings, too. However, many experts questioned Foster's claim for one very important reason, Kurin told CNN.

"He didn't have Thomas Jefferson's DNA," Kurin said. "He didn't have something to directly compare living descendants of the Jefferson family to Madison Hemings and Eston Hemings and others that might have been the descendants of Thomas Jefferson." Critics of that the 1998 study said Foster's evidence merely connected Hemings' descendants to a male in the Jefferson lineage, and not necessarily to the former president.

"I thought, if we can get Thomas Jefferson's DNA, we could use that as the source of comparison to various descendants, and really firmly solve the question," Kurin said.

Kurin and his team were initially disappointed to find that the Bible hair wasn't the smoking gun that they thought it would be. To check whether the hair was Jefferson's, they compared its DNA with that of a living woman who was a direct descendant of Thomas Jefferson's mother along the family's female lineage. They expected to find identical mitochondrial DNA, which is genetic material specifically inherited from the maternal side. But their hopes were dashed when the two samples didn't match.

Still, they were able to access other hair samples that records attributed to Thomas Jefferson. These hairs, including a lock clipped at his deathbed, were in a packet provided by the Thomas Jefferson Foundation at Monticello, and had not previously been available for analysis. The scientists reconstructed and compared historic genome sequences of Jefferson and Hemings with DNA collected from 16 living individuals, including multiple descendants of Eston and Madison Hemings. These analyses found matches across genomes that linked Hemings descendants to Thomas Jefferson.

"What made this study so powerful is that researchers weren't just comparing two genomes," said Éadaoin Harney, a senior population geneticist at the 23andMe Research Institute. "Instead, they collected DNA samples from multiple people from different branches of the family tree."

In genetic analysis, larger sample pools provide more robust conclusions, said Harney, who was not involved in the new research. "By studying the patterns of DNA sharing across all of these individuals, it became possible to disambiguate exactly how the descendants of Sally Hemings were related to Thomas Jefferson," she told CNN in an email.

While the new book and paper focus on genomic data of well-known historical figures, these methods are also broadly useful for illuminating the obscured history of enslaved people, which has been a focus of Harney's own research. In a 2023 study of enslaved and free African Americans from Maryland, Harney used DNA analysis combined with other biomolecular and archaeological techniques to uncover individuals' ancestry and places of origin. The data also suggested links to people who still live in Maryland.

"Historical records are full of gaps, particularly when it comes to documenting the lives of people who occupied less privileged places in society," she said. "This is particularly true for enslaved Africans and African Americans, who are often only described in historical records as property."

Genetic analyses, such as those used in the new Jefferson study, can help restore connections that were lost because of slavery, Harney added. "The same tools can be applied to study the many enslaved people whose lives were never well documented, and help reconnect them with their descendants."

Whispers about Jefferson's sexual relationship with Hemings — who was 30 years his junior and a half-sister to his wife — have endured for more than 200 years. Initial rumors were fueled by local innuendo and supported by records aligning Hemings' pregnancies with Jefferson's presence at his plantation home of Monticello in Virginia. An article published in 1902 in the Richmond Recorder stated that "there is not an individual in the neighbourhood of Charlottesville who does not believe the story," regarding Jefferson fathering children with Hemings.

Though the conclusions of Foster's 1998 study were not universally accepted, that genetic evidence was compelling enough for the Thomas Jefferson Foundation to issue a statement two years later acknowledging "the strong likelihood that Thomas Jefferson and Sally Hemings had a relationship over time that led to the birth of one, and perhaps all, of the known children of Sally Hemings."

Finally laying that uncertainty to rest was enough of a motivation to keep Kurin and the other researchers going for more than a decade, despite their initial disappointment that the hair found in the Bible did not belong to Thomas Jefferson, he said.

"We had hit a dead end, but scientists are always looking for alternatives," he said. "I think we were propelled still by scientific and historical curiosity."

While the question of Jefferson's ancestry in Hemings' descendants may finally have been answered, another remains: Whose hair was pressed in Jefferson's bible? The researchers had collected enough of its fragmentary genetic data to know that it belonged to a female member of the Jefferson family, but that was all the information the team could learn, Kurin said.

"It's like a partial fingerprint," he explained. "That is still a lingering mystery."

Mindy Weisberger is a science writer and media producer whose work has appeared in Live Science, Scientific American and How It Works magazine. She is the author of " Rise of the Zombie Bugs : The Surprising Science of Parasitic Mind-Control" (Hopkins Press).

articles.title: 12-million-year-old fossil leaf from the Himalaya reveals a previously unknown fungal species
articles.summary: A fossilised leaf from the western Himalaya has preserved a previously unknown fungal species that lived around 12 to 8 million years ago.
articles.body: A fossilised leaf from the western Himalaya has preserved a previously unknown fungal species that lived around 12 to 8 million years ago. The fungus, Vizellopsidites miocenicus, was found on a fossilised dicot leaf recovered from the middle Siwalik sediments of Himachal Pradesh.Researchers Sampa Kundu and Mahasin Ali Khan described the species in a study published in the New Zealand Journal of Botany titled ‘A New Epifoliar Fossil Fungal Species, Vizellopsidites miocenicus, From India’. The fungus covered the upper surface of the leaf cuticle with a distinctive network of dark brown structures. Its position on the leaf also preserved evidence of an ectoparasite relationship between the fungus and its host plant in the warm, humid tropical Siwalik forest of the Himachal Himalaya.A new fossil fungus was found on a Miocene leafThe newly described species is Vizellopsidites miocenicus sp. nov., an epifoliar ascomycotal fossil fungal species. It was recovered from the middle Siwalik sediments of Himachal Pradesh in the western Himalaya. The sediments date to the Late Miocene, around 12 to 8 million years ago. The fossil fungus was preserved on the adaxial surfaces of cuticular fragments from a fossilised dicot leaf.Researchers identified features that distinguish the fossil while also noting similarities with modern fungal forms. Its mycelium morphology is similar to that of modern Vizellopsis Bat., Bezerra and Barros., while its sporocarp morphology resembles Vizella Sacc. The discovery adds a new fossil species to the record of fungi preserved on ancient leaves from the Indian Himalaya.What did the fossil fungus look likeThe fossil fungus had superficial or intracuticular hyphae arranged in a reticulate pattern across the leaf surface. These hyphae were laterally branched and dark brown. They were also septate, which means the fungal structures contained internal divisions. The hyphal cells were squarish to rectangular and were often irregular in shape. Their septa were strongly constricted and dark. Along with the mycelial mat, the fossil preserved circular thyriothecioid sporocarps.These reproductive structures had a centrally placed ostiole beneath the mycelial mat. The combination of these features was used to describe Vizellopsidites miocenicus as a new fossil fungal species. The researchers documented the structures in situ on the fossilised leaf cuticle, preserving the relationship between the fungus and its plant host.How was the fungus linked to the ancient leafThe position of the fungal structures on the fossilised dicot leaf provided evidence of an association between the fungus and its host plant. The fossil fungus occurred directly on the leaf cuticular fragments rather than being found separately from the plant material. The study identifies this in situ evidence as indicating an ectoparasite relationship between the dicot host and Vizellopsidites miocenicus.This means the preserved material records the fungus living in association with the leaf. The finding is important within the fossil record because the fungus and its host were preserved together. The researchers were able to examine the fungal structures in their original position on the leaf surface, rather than relying only on isolated fossil fungal remains.What does the fossil reveal about the ancient forestThe fossil was recovered from middle Siwalik sediments deposited during the Late Miocene, around 12 to 8 million years ago. According to the study, the in situ preservation of Vizellopsidites miocenicus indicates that an ectoparasite relationship existed in the tropical Siwalik forest of the Himachal Himalaya during the time of deposition. The researchers describe the forest as warm and humid.The fossil preserves evidence not only of a previously unknown fungal species but also of its relationship with a dicot plant in that ancient environment. The discovery adds another record of fossil fungi associated with leaves from the Siwalik region.

articles.title: Ontario will permanently protect 969 acres at Echo Lake, where more than 400 wildlife species are already documented; the land is planned to return to Garden River First Nation stewardship within five years
articles.summary: At the edge of Echo Lake in northern Ontario, a stretch of forest, wetlands, cliffs and waterways is set to become more than protected wilderness.
articles.body: At the edge of Echo Lake in northern Ontario, a stretch of forest, wetlands, cliffs and waterways is set to become more than protected wilderness. It is also part of a larger effort to restore Indigenous stewardship over land with deep cultural roots. Nearly 1,000 acres at the lake's northeast end will now be protected through a partnership involving Garden River First Nation, the Central Algoma Land Trust and Ontario Nature, states an online report by Sootoday.The 392-hectare property in Kehoe Township will become the Paswe Protected Area, establishing what the partners describe as the region's first Indigenous Protected and Conserved Area. Paswe is the Anishinaabemowin name for echo, explains the online report.Returning land to Indigenous stewardshipThe property carries significance that extends beyond its ecological value. It was historically part of the Garden River First Nation reserve before colonial-era government reductions altered the community's original boundaries, explains the online report. And under the new arrangement, the Central Algoma Land Trust will initially hold legal title to the property for five years. The partners intend to then transfer administrative ownership permanently to Garden River First Nation.During the transition, the First Nation's Guardian Unit will play a central role in managing the land. Its responsibilities will include ecological monitoring, species-at-risk surveys, trail maintenance and supporting community-led ceremonies and traditional harvesting. The arrangement is designed to combine conservation with the cultural responsibilities associated with the landscape, while maintaining sustainable public access.A critical wildlife corridorAs per the online report, Paswe Protected Area sits within the Bawating and Ketegaunseebee Ecocultural Corridor, a priority cultural and ecological landscape identified by Garden River First Nation, Ontario Nature and other regional partners. The property borders the existing Garden River First Nation reserve and Crown land, connecting directly with more than 20,000 hectares of largely natural territory within the reserve. That continuity creates a substantial wilderness corridor and an important route for wildlife moving across the region.The landscape itself is varied. Mature forests rise around tall cliffs, while wetlands provide additional habitat. The property includes a significant section of the Upper Echo River, which holds deep cultural importance for Garden River First Nation, as well as shorelines along Echo Lake and most of Fairy Lake.More than 400 species already recordedEven before a comprehensive inventory has been completed, researchers and conservation partners have documented more than 400 wildlife species across the property. The area provides confirmed or potential habitat for several species at risk, including lake sturgeon, peregrine falcons, Canada warblers and wood thrushes. It also contains stands of black ash, a culturally important tree species that has faced growing ecological pressures, adds the report.Water protection is another major focus. Garden River First Nation is leading an aquatic restoration project in the Upper Echo River basin, with government support, aimed at improving habitat connectivity, restoring native fisheries and managing invasive species.Public access will continueAs explained in the Sootodya report, protection of the property will not mean closing it off. The partners plan to maintain responsible, low-impact public access, including hiking along the Voyageur Trail, which crosses the area. A detailed management plan is expected to be developed in the coming months. It will establish guidelines for recreation, trail maintenance, ecological monitoring and cultural protection.The result will be a conservation model that links biodiversity protection with Indigenous land stewardship, while keeping the landscape accessible for future generations.Images Courtesy: istock

articles.title: En 2021, liberaron 25 águilas noruegas en España, cinco años después siguen causando polémica: "Puede ocasionar graves problemas a especies amenazadas"
articles.standfirst: La reintroducción de esta especie divide a los ecologistas
articles.summary: La reintroducción de esta especie divide a los ecologistas
articles.body: En el año 2021, un grupo de conservación comenzó la liberación de 25 ejemplares de pigargo europeo (Haliaeetus albicilla) procedentes de Noruega en el entorno natural de Asturias. El objetivo declarado era recuperar en la península ibérica a la considerada el águila más grande de Europa, aprovechando su inclusión en el catálogo nacional de especies extinguidas. Sin embargo, la iniciativa ha intensificado un acalorado debate entre biólogos, colectivos ecologistas y administraciones sobre la oportunidad real de esta medida. Los defensores del proyecto, liderados por la asociación GREFA, argumentan que existen indicios históricos e idoneidad de hábitat suficientes para reintroducir este superdepredador, señalando que la especie ejerce una función valiosa como limpiadora del ecosistema. Frente a esta postura, numerosos expertos e instituciones científicas cuestionan la base jurídica y biológica del plan. Sostienen que no existen pruebas concluyentes de que el pigargo haya mantenido poblaciones estables y nidificantes en territorio español en épocas recientes. A esta discrepancia se suma el estado global de la especie, catalogada por la Unión Internacional para la Conservación de la Naturaleza (UICN) bajo la categoría de "preocupación menor" debido a sus abundantes poblaciones en Escandinavia y el centro de Europa. Por ello, los sectores críticos consideran inoportuno dedicar esfuerzos y recursos a introducir una ave cuya conservación mundial no peligra y que actúa en la práctica como una especie exótica no autóctona. La principal preocupación reside en el impacto trófico que este depredador voraz genera sobre el frágil ecosistema del norte de España. Con una dieta amplia basada en aves acuáticas, mamíferos y peces, los opositores advierten de que “puede ocasionar graves problemas a especies amenazadas” que ya sufren un deterioro crítico de sus hábitats. Un caso especialmente delicado es el del salmón atlántico en las cuencas de Asturias y Cantabria, cuyos cauces registran declives mínimos históricos debido al calentamiento del agua, las alteraciones del caudal y la sobrepesca. La presencia del pigargo supone sumar una fuerte presión sobre unas poblaciones salmoneras golpeadas. Cinco años después de su llegada, la polémica se mantiene viva entre quienes defienden la reintroducción de esta majestuosa ave y quienes alertan del riesgo inminente para la biodiversidad ibérica amenazada.

articles.title: En 2002, ingenieros depositaron 1,8 millones de yardas cúbicas de sedimentos: formaron una isla de 35 hectáreas
articles.standfirst: Un proyecto iniciado en Luisiana aprovechó la fuerza de la corriente para transformarlo en un nuevo espacio natural
articles.summary: Un proyecto iniciado en Luisiana aprovechó la fuerza de la corriente para transformarlo en un nuevo espacio natural
articles.body: Lo que durante décadas había sido un problema de mantenimiento terminó convirtiéndose en una curiosa solución de ingeniería. En el río Atchafalaya, en Luisiana (Estados Unidos), los ingenieros necesitaban retirar periódicamente grandes cantidades de sedimentos acumulados en el canal de navegación. En lugar de limitarse a desecharlos, decidieron utilizarlos para favorecer la expansión de una pequeña isla que ya estaba formándose de manera natural. El proyecto comenzó en 2002, cuando el Cuerpo de Ingenieros del Ejército de Estados Unidos empezó a colocar estratégicamente el material dragado en una zona situada aguas arriba de la isla. Cada entre uno y tres años se depositaban aproximadamente entre 0,5 y 1,8 millones de yardas cúbicas de sedimentos, que equivalen a cientos de miles de metros cúbicos. La clave estaba precisamente en no intentar construir la isla de forma convencional. Los sedimentos se acumulaban en determinados puntos y después era la propia corriente del río la que los desplazaba y distribuía. Con el paso del tiempo, este proceso permitió que la superficie de tierra aumentara hasta alcanzar aproximadamente 35 hectáreas. El resultado llamó la atención de los investigadores porque el nuevo territorio no quedó simplemente como una acumulación de barro y arena. La isla comenzó a desarrollar distintos tipos de hábitats y fue colonizada por numerosas especies vegetales y animales. Los estudios realizados por investigadores del propio Cuerpo de Ingenieros identificaron cuatro tipos de hábitat y una elevada presencia de vegetación autóctona. También aparecieron beneficios para las aves. Las características del terreno favorecieron la creación de una importante zona de reproducción para aves zancudas, mientras que los nuevos ambientes acuáticos permitieron la presencia de una amplia variedad de invertebrados. Los análisis del suelo también encontraron funciones relacionadas con la retención de nutrientes y la mejora de la calidad del agua. Pero había otro objetivo. Al crecer la isla, disminuyó parte de la sección transversal del río y aumentó la velocidad del agua en el canal de navegación. Esto ayudó a reducir la acumulación de sedimentos y, por tanto, las necesidades de determinados trabajos de dragado posteriores. Lo que comenzó como una forma diferente de gestionar el material extraído durante el mantenimiento del río terminó convirtiéndose en un ejemplo de “ingeniería con la naturaleza”: utilizar los propios procesos naturales para transformar un residuo de una obra en un nuevo ecosistema.

articles.title: Elon Musk's 'tip' to tech CEOs: Best way to test 'safety' of your AI models is to put them on a Delta flight, as ...
articles.summary: Elon Musk has humorously suggested that the best way to test the safety of AI models is by placing them on a Delta flight, implying that the airline's
articles.body: Elon Musk has humorously suggested that the best way to test the safety of AI models is by placing them on a Delta flight, implying that the airline's in-flight WiFi is so unreliable it effectively cuts off internet access. Sharing a post on X (formerly Twitter), Musk wrote:“Best way to sandbox an AI is to put it on a Delta flight – it will have no chance of accessing the Internet!”. The comments come as Delta Airlines opted against Starlink in favour of Amazon Leo for in-flight internet service. According to latest reports, Delta CEO Ed Bastian cited Elon Musk as the reason to skip Starlink. An X user JonNYC allegedly cited the Delta CEO saying “We do not want to be with Elon Musk”.Elon Musk warns Delta will ‘lose a lot of customers’In a post on September 28, X user John LeFevre said that Delta's rival United Airlines Holdings Inc. had 600+ aircraft with Starlink. The figure represented approximately 36% of the airline's entire fleet. "Delta has zero, and no plans for it. People will book accordingly. RIP Delta," he wrote in the post.SpaceX CEO Elon Musk responded to the post writing: “Delta will lose a lot of customers”.Delta Airlines on why it rejected Elon Musk’s StarlinkDelta Airlines is reportedly targeting 2028 to start offering Leo in-flight Wi-Fi on about half of its fleet. As quoted in a post by X user Sawyer Meritt earlier this year, Delta Airlines explained why it chose Amazon’s Leo saying:“This agreement gives us the fastest and most cost-effective technology available to better connect the world today, and it deepens our work with a global leader that shares our ambition to build what’s next.”In a statement to PC Mag then, the airline said “The assertion in question is not accurate”, claiming that incorporating Delta Sync with Starlink would have been permitted under SpaceX's in-flight Wi-Fi agreement. articles.title: AT&T CEO John Stankey 'agrees' with T-Mobile CEO Peter Osvaldik that Elon Musk's plans to shake up mobile industry with Starlink should be laughed out of the room
articles.summary: AT&T CEO John Stankey has sided with T-Mobile’s chief executive Peter Osvaldik in rejecting Elon Musk’s plan to disrupt the mobile industry with Starlink.
articles.body: AT&T CEO John Stankey has sided with T-Mobile’s chief executive Peter Osvaldik in rejecting Elon Musk’s plan to disrupt the mobile industry with Starlink. Speaking to Axios, Stankey said SpaceX’s proposal to turn its satellite business into a global competitor to traditional telecom networks is “not a viable strategy.” He argued that fiber infrastructure remains superior, noting AT&T’s $3 billion deal with Corning to expand its fiber footprint. Earlier this month, T-Mobile CEO Peter Osvaldik dismissed Musk’s Starlink ambitions outright, and said that the strategy should be “laughed out of the room.” Osvaldik said Starlink’s approach lacked the scale and economics to compete with established carriers, reinforcing skepticism across the telecom industry.What T-Mobile CEO Peter Osvaldik said firstT-Mobile CFO Peter Osvaldik was blunt in his own assessment of Starlink's mobile ambitions, saying that "everybody in the know" is laughing at parts of the plan, and describing SpaceX's proposal as something that isn't fathomable from a technical standpoint. He argued Starlink doesn't represent a real competitive threat from a wireless perspective, pointing to basic physics as the core obstacle: satellite signals, he said, can't penetrate buildings, walls, or even something as simple as a car windshield, making Starlink's direct-to-cell ambitions far less practical in dense urban environments than in the remote areas where satellite coverage genuinely shines.AT&T CEO John Stankey's rebuttal: Fiber beats satellite, full stopSpeaking to Axios, Stankey made a similarly confident case for why AT&T isn't worried, backing it with a major infrastructure move. AT&T announced a $3 billion deal with Corning this week to expand its fiber infrastructure, arguing that fiber delivers speeds three times faster than satellite technology. Stankey didn't mince words about the comparison, saying nothing beats fiber, and that even if satellite technology performs at its absolute best over the next decade, it still won't be able to match what fiber delivers.Why the rivalry is heating upThe pushback from both carriers comes as Musk and SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell have been increasingly vocal about turning Starlink into a genuine competitor to traditional phone and internet providers. Starlink already competes with legacy telecom companies for home and business internet customers, and the company has now started talking openly about a mobile business that would put it in direct competition with wireless carriers.Shotwell added fuel to that narrative in August, during SpaceX's first earnings call as a public company, predicting that SpaceX would be able to win over a meaningful number of customers from existing carriers because its service would simply be better. That comment rattled markets, sending shares of AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile lower the following day.The scale of Starlink's ambitionsAs of June 30, Starlink had 12 million subscribers and more than 10,200 satellites providing coverage across 167 countries, according to SpaceX's first earnings report as a public company. While SpaceX's rockets and AI work tend to dominate headlines, its connectivity business is actually the company's largest revenue driver, accounting for 55% of total sales.Becoming a genuine fourth major US mobile carrier, however, would require significantly more terrestrial infrastructure to match the capacity of a traditional cellular network — a build-out one analyst estimated could cost SpaceX more than $100 billion. SpaceX believes it has found a cheaper alternative: installing small cellular base stations alongside Starlink dishes at homes and businesses, adding capacity where satellite coverage alone falls short, without needing to build the kind of sprawling cell tower network traditional carriers rely on. Musk has claimed these small stations could eventually deliver connectivity to phones with better and higher bandwidth than what's currently available from existing cellular providers.Why Stankey says the math doesn't workStankey pushed back hard on that plan's feasibility, arguing that installing enough small stations to match a traditional network's capacity would cost roughly the same as simply building a full macro cellular network. He also pointed to a significant regulatory hurdle: current law doesn't allow companies to radiate cellular signals from someone's home without their permission, unless that law changes. He suggested that if the approach were genuinely viable and cost-effective, AT&T would already be installing similar antennas across its own massive existing fiber network.You use AI every day. articles.title: 20 African wild dogs were brought back to a Zimbabwe park after disappearing for decades; conservationists rebuilt the ecosystem before their return
articles.summary: African wild dogs returned to Zimbabwe’s Matusadona National Park in February 2026 after disappearing from the area for decades.
articles.body: African wild dogs returned to Zimbabwe’s Matusadona National Park in February 2026 after disappearing from the area for decades. 20 animals were moved into the park in two established packs, marking a major step in the restoration of a predator that had been locally extinct there. But the return did not begin with the release itself. African Parks and the Zimbabwe Parks and Wildlife Management Authority had spent years rebuilding protection, wildlife populations, monitoring systems and community links across Matusadona before the dogs arrived.How 20 African wild dogs returned to Matusadona after decadesThe 20 African wild dogs were translocated between 15 and 17 February 2026, according to African Parks. The animals came from Nuanetsi Ranch in southern Zimbabwe and were moved in 2 established packs, with 6 dogs in one and 14 in the other.The operation was led by African Parks and the Zimbabwe Parks and Wildlife Management Authority, or ZimParks. NineDaysinEden reported that the process involved wildlife specialists, veterinarians, aircraft crews and conservation teams, with the animals undergoing health checks and careful monitoring before transport.The dogs were not released straight into the wider park. Instead, they were placed in specially built holding facilities near Tashinga for several weeks. This soft-release approach gave the packs time to recover from the journey, become familiar with their surroundings, maintain their social bonds and begin establishing a connection with the new territory.Matusadona was rebuilt before these predators arrivedThe return of the dogs followed 5 years of conservation work in the park. African Parks said its partnership with ZimParks was formalised in 2020, after which efforts focused on strengthening anti-poaching systems, ranger training, biodiversity monitoring, infrastructure and community programmes.Wildlife restoration was also part of that work. According to African Parks, zebra, buffalo, sable and eland had been moved into the park as part of efforts to rebuild its wildlife populations and restore the wider ecosystem.This preparation mattered because wild dogs need more than a protected patch of land. SafariFind reported that the species generally requires large, connected landscapes with enough prey and relatively low levels of direct persecution. Packs can travel beyond park boundaries, making cooperation with neighbouring communities and land managers important to their survival.Importance of wild dogs to the restored ecosystemAfrican wild dogs are among Africa’s most endangered large carnivores. African Parks puts the number remaining in the wild at fewer than 7,000, while its detailed species information gives an approximate figure of 6,600.Their importance is not limited to being a rare wildlife sighting. They are highly social predators that hunt cooperatively and help regulate prey populations. The African Bush Camps Foundation said their return contributes to restoring the ecological balance of Matusadona.The species faces several threats across Zimbabwe and elsewhere. SafariFind identifies habitat fragmentation, snares, disease, conflict with people, road deaths and declining prey as continuing pressures. Wild dogs can also travel through communal areas and private land, meaning conservation efforts cannot stop at the boundaries of a national park.GPS tracking will help keep the packs safeThe newly introduced dogs are being closely watched as they settle into Matusadona. African Parks reported that all adult wild dogs were fitted with GPS collars so their movements and social behaviour can be followed.The park has also introduced a GPS-based geofence warning system around nearby settlements. When collared wildlife approaches these areas, alerts can be triggered so conservation teams can respond before animals move into inhabited locations.African Parks reported that 12 rangers from Nyaminyami Rural District Council have been brought into the park’s operational structure, while 8 Human-Wildlife Conflict Ward Monitors are working in important areas of neighbouring chiefdoms. The monitors provide an early-warning link between communities and park authorities and can report incidents quickly.The return forms part of a wider recoveryMatusadona covers 1,470 square kilometres along the southern shores of Lake Kariba, according to African Parks. Its habitats include floodplains, the drowned forest and the Zambezi Escarpment, supporting animals such as elephants, buffalo, lions and leopards as well as more than 240 bird species.The wild dogs are therefore returning to a landscape where broader restoration work is already under way. African Parks said their reintroduction also supports conservation across the wider Sebungwe region.SafariFind estimates about 660 wild dogs in 86 packs across the country, although it notes that figures vary according to surveys and sources. Important populations remain in the Greater Hwange Ecosystem, the Zambezi Valley and the south-east lowveld.The long-term outcome for the Matusadona packs will depend on what happens after their release. African Parks said the team will continue tracking their movements, social dynamics and adaptation, with the information helping in future management.

articles.title: Young minds in Ipswich develop ideas to tackle climate change
articles.summary: Sixteen teenagers take part in a hackathon to devise ways to combat issues such as light pollution.
articles.body:
A group of young people have developed ideas to tackle the effects of climate change as part of a free touring exhibition.

On Tuesday 16 young people took part in a hackathon - a timed event where people work together to build creative solutions to problems - where they devised posters with ways to combat light pollution, wild fires, damage to oceans and poor water quality.

The event was hosted by Seeds of Hope and Change, an organisation run by the Soka Gakkai International and the UN Earth Charter, at the Jerwood Dancehouse in Ipswich.

Maryanne, 16, took part in the project and said: "We just want people to be aware of what's going on, especially with major issues such as ocean pollution."

Climate change is the long-term shift in the Earth's average temperatures and weather conditions.

This year's summer was the UK's hottest on record, according to provisional data from the Met Office .

The Met Office said the heat experienced this summer was made about 130 times more likely by human-induced climate change.

Baveen, 17, said "We wanted to talk about the cities and the sky and how it affects people and also wildlife."

The poster her group produced included ideas for using low-intensity bulbs and motion sensors in street lights so that they were not continuously left on.

The exhibition, which is free and runs until 4 October, includes 24 pop-up panels that share information and environmental case studies from around the world on the impact of climate change.

The hackathon for young people was run by ambassadors from the youth-led campaigning organisation #iWill.

Alex Harrison, one of the #iWill ambassadors, said: "The main purpose is reminding young people that in the face of something really scary like climate change, there's a lot that you can do personally to make a real change."
